title: ML Platform
seoTitle: Design a Machine Learning Platform and ML Data Pipeline
description: Design an internal machine learning platform — data pipelines and a feature store, distributed training jobs, experiment tracking, a model registry, and online serving with monitoring.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is an ML Platform?
blocks.text: An ML platform (like Uber's Michelangelo or the tooling behind SageMaker and Vertex AI) gives data scientists one paved road from raw data to a model in production: pipelines that turn data into features, infrastructure to train models, a registry to version them, and serving to make predictions — with monitoring to catch when models go stale. This page also covers designing the **data pipeline for an ML application**, which is the first half of the platform.

items: Teams should be able to define features once and use them for both training and online prediction.
Teams should be able to launch training jobs on CPUs/GPUs and track experiments (parameters, metrics, artefacts).
Trained models should be versioned in a registry and promoted to production.
Production services should get low-latency online predictions; batch predictions should also be supported.
Models should be monitored for data drift and prediction quality.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: No training/serving skew: a feature has the same value logic offline and online.
Online prediction latency < 20 ms p99 including feature lookup.
Reproducibility: any model can be traced to its exact data, code and parameters.
Efficient use of expensive GPUs across many teams.
Scale to hundreds of models and ~100k predictions per second.
**Feature**: a named, versioned transformation (e.g. `user_orders_7d`) with an entity key.
**Dataset**: a point-in-time snapshot of features and labels used for training.
**Training run**: code version, data snapshot, hyperparameters, metrics, artefacts.
**Model version**: a registered artefact with lineage and stage (`staging`, `production`).

blocks.text: 1) Data pipelines and the feature store

Raw data arrives from service databases (via CDC) and event streams into a **data lake**. Feature pipelines — **batch** (Spark) for slow-moving features and **streaming** (Flink) for fresh ones — compute features from one shared definition. Results go to two stores: an **offline store** (the lake, keeping full history for training) and an **online store** (Redis/DynamoDB, latest value per entity for serving).

A data scientist requests a training dataset with **point-in-time joins** (feature values as they were at each label's timestamp, never from the future). The **training service** schedules the job on a GPU cluster (Kubernetes with a batch scheduler), and the run logs parameters, metrics and artefacts to an **experiment tracker**.
The best run is registered as a **model version** with full lineage: code commit, dataset snapshot, feature versions and metrics. Promotion to production requires passing evaluation gates.

The **model server** loads the production version. For each request it fetches the entity's features from the online store, runs the model, and returns the prediction. Every prediction and its features are **logged**, so monitoring can compare live feature distributions to training data (drift) and join predictions with later outcomes to measure accuracy.
1) How do we prevent training/serving skew?

blocks.title: Separate code for training and serving

approach.text: Data scientists compute features in notebooks; engineers reimplement them in the serving service.

challenges.text: The two implementations drift apart, and the model silently performs worse in production than offline.

approach.text: Features are defined once in the feature store and the same definition generates both the offline backfill and the online pipeline.

challenges.text: Still possible to leak future data into training if joins aren't time-aware.

approach.text: Training datasets use **point-in-time joins** against the offline store's history, so each training example sees only what would have been known then. In addition, the serving layer **logs the exact features it used** for each prediction; future training data can be built from these logs, guaranteeing training matches serving exactly.

challenges.text: Logging every feature vector is a large data volume — sample for high-traffic models.

blocks.text: 2) How do we share GPUs across teams?

GPUs are scarce and expensive. A **cluster scheduler** with per-team **quotas** and **priority** classes runs jobs; low-priority jobs can borrow idle capacity and are **preempted** when owners need it, so training code must **checkpoint** regularly. Gang scheduling makes sure a distributed job gets all its GPUs at once rather than holding half of them idle.
Mention that checkpointing turns preemption from a disaster into a minor delay — the job resumes from its last checkpoint.
3) How do we deploy models safely?

Promotion goes through **shadow mode** (the new model scores live traffic but its predictions aren't used), then a **canary** taking a small share of traffic with metrics compared against the current model, then full rollout. Rollback is switching the endpoint back to the previous version, which stays loaded for a while.

quiz.question: What is training/serving skew?
options: Features computed differently in training and production, degrading the live model
quiz.explanation: Shared definitions and logged features prevent it.

quiz.question: Why use point-in-time joins for training data?
options: So each example only sees feature values known at that time, avoiding leakage
quiz.explanation: Future information in training makes offline metrics misleadingly good.

quiz.question: Why does a feature store have both offline and online stores?
options: Training needs full history; serving needs the latest value in milliseconds
quiz.explanation: Different access patterns need different storage.

quiz.question: What makes GPU preemption tolerable for training jobs?
options: Regular checkpoints so jobs resume where they left off
quiz.explanation: Checkpointing lets the scheduler share GPUs aggressively.
